newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China reforms seen trimming cotton prices, stocks.
newsitem.headline: China reforms seen trimming cotton prices, stocks.

text.p: Bejing's plan to reform its agricultural system will probably reduce huge stockpiles of cotton choking the market and soften artifically high domestic prices, cotton analysts and traders said on Friday.
"I think the policy is clearly aimed at getting local stocks moved and imports reduced," said a cotton expert in Hong Kong.

Li Tieying, minister in charge of China's State Commission for Restructuring the Economy, announced in a speech in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen this week that market forces were to govern cotton buying in future.
"China has decided to use cotton trade fairs...to replace the state-planned system," a government official, who declined to be identified, said on Thursday.
In fact, China's stagnant cotton market had already shown signs of loosening up over the past couple of months as interprovincial trade has increased and domestic prices softened, traders said.
"We have recently noticed that the cotton market has freed up to a considerable extent, in the sense that there is quite a lot of interprovincial trading going on," one source said.
Traders reported that the domestic price of cotton in the western province of Xinjiang had dipped to between 18,000 to 18,500 yuan a tonne from about 19,500 yuan six weeks go.
"Local prices have come down to a more feasible level," one cotton source said, noting this was largely a result of freed up trade in cotton from domestic stockpiles.
In some areas, cotton prices were below the permitted four percent fluctuation band established by the government in September this year, according to one source.

"When they stipulated the policy for this year, they said that contrary to previous years, when the price to the mills was fixed, this year the price could fluctuate plus or minus four percent above or below," the cotton expert said.
At the same time, rising international prices were making cotton from the U.S. and Australia less attractive to Chinese textile mills.

"Good to middling cotton costs Chinese mills about 85.50 US cents per pound (15,648 yuan per tonne), C&F Chinese main port," a trader said, noting that higher costs would hurt profit margins for importers.

"With U.S. cotton in the 85 cent area, that will curtail imports," another source said, noting he had slashed his import estimates for 1996/97 (August-July) to 1.8 million bales, down from 2.5 million bales the previous year.

China's cotton industry has suffered as the government purchased cotton from farmers at artificially high prices, making the raw material too expensive for textile millers who then turned to cheaper imports.
But cotton exporters in India said they believe the Chinese move could open the market for more sales.

"Indian cotton is already going to China through Hong Kong. The latest developments in China will give a fillip to India's cotton exports to that country," said Suresh Kotak, president of the East India Cotton Association, a traders' organisation.
A bumper cotton harvest has put India in a strong position to export large quantities in the 1996/97 season (October/September), traders said.
They estimate India's 1996/97 cotton crop at 16 million bales, about the same as in the previous year, during which the government authorised an export of 1.59 million bales.
New Delhi recently authorised exports of 500,000 bales of cotton at the beginning of the season. Traders said at least another million bales should also be available for export.
